episode_thesis: David Harding (Winton) argues that every successful strategy attracts capital until its edge decays, so trend following in futures, once a Sharpe-near-1 machine for 30 years, has become crowded beta and a firm must keep innovating: Winton is moving weight into a 7,000-stock global equity book (event, organizational-metric and customised technical strategies) built on cloud computing and long research cycles. He holds that markets are an evolving ecosystem rather than efficient atoms in a box, that government macro data are too heavily revised to trade on, that trend following is not a dependable crash hedge, and that leverage was cut because crowding plus fat tails creates catastrophe risk.

speakers.name: David Harding
speakers.role: Founder and head of Winton (systematic CTA / quant manager)
speakers.speaker_note: Interview is Bloomberg Television, 2019-03-18, with an unnamed interviewer who addresses him as 'David'; interviewer questions are context only and no interviewer view is mapped. Captions are unpunctuated auto-captions; one phrase ('i'm 100 comment') is a caption garble and is not used as a quote. Figures such as 5 billion redeemed appear in the interviewer's question, not as Harding's claim.

worldview_premises.premise: Any business or strategy that succeeds without a monopoly attracts too much capital, which drives returns down and forces innovation; crowding degrades return-to-risk.
worldview_premises.support: General economic reasoning; own experience as trend following became crowded.

worldview_premises.premise: Markets are an evolving ecosystem (jungle), not atoms in a box: edges are never perfect, they decay and new ones emerge, so mathematics stays useful but must be renewed.
worldview_premises.support: Metaphor and contrast with efficient market theory; no data.

worldview_premises.premise: Simple trend rules have lost their old edge as they became accessible 'beta': fast futures versions crowded first, slower ones now.
worldview_premises.support: Winton's own history of getting slower; the 1980s moving-average crossover anecdote.

worldview_premises.premise: Part of the apparent decline in hedge fund returns is mechanical: near-zero cash rates (6% in the 80s-90s) and halved leverage, so adjusted track records look similar to the past.
worldview_premises.support: Arithmetic: double the track record and add 6%.

worldview_premises.premise: Crowdedness together with fat tails creates the risk of overnight catastrophic moves (LTCM, 2008), so leverage should be conservative, especially for unsophisticated clients.
worldview_premises.support: LTCM and 2008 episodes; own use of about 2x gross versus ~10x rumoured at Goldman Global Alpha.

worldview_premises.premise: Government macro statistics are revised so often and so heavily that long time series of them are unreliable inputs for systematic macro; PMI forecasting could not be proven in available data.
worldview_premises.support: US 2009 double dip erased nine years later; Japan growth estimates 0.4 vs 2.5; a two-year multi-million-pound PMI study was inconclusive.

worldview_premises.premise: Futures trend-following rules do not carry over unchanged to equities; stocks need event, governance/organizational and customised technical strategies, though some momentum know-how transfers.
worldview_premises.support: Winton's own attempt ('a graveyard of companies that have tried').

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following is a statistical, unpredictable system that cannot be timed; it is not a reliable crash hedge because it is long after rallies, and would aggravate a 1987-style fall.
worldview_premises.support: 2008 and 2001-02 helped; 1987-style crashes and Feb 2018 (managed futures long and lost) did not.

worldview_premises.premise: Volatility is not trending higher; percent volatility peaked in 1933-34 and nominal point charts mislead, while low-volatility periods can precede crises.
worldview_premises.support: Historical charts in log terms; 2006-07 low vol before the crisis.

worldview_premises.premise: Volatility is a voluntary commercial choice set by leverage (a 'volume knob'), independent of which strategies are used.

The hedge fund industry has been sustained by beta from the long equity bull market; active managers without real edge face growing pressure as performance gets measured and as many discretionary strategies prove automatable.
worldview_premises.support: Industry observation; trend following as an example of automated discretion.

worldview_premises.premise: Quant progress is slow and secretive because there is no IP protection and no publication; cumulative team research (Renaissance) rather than a single data item is what creates edge.
worldview_premises.support: Own experience and reasoning about Renaissance.

worldview_premises.premise: AI is one part reality and nine parts hype; algorithm responsibility must remain with named humans, and computing (cloud) helps research scale more than 'intelligence' does.
worldview_premises.support: Own view; deep learning progress noted but not general intelligence.

steps.from: Trend following earns a Sharpe near 1 for about 30 years
steps.to: Capital and competitors pile into the strategy
steps.why: Success attracts money; the strategy is easy to replicate and seen as beta.

steps.from: Crowding in fast then slower futures trend systems
steps.why: Too much money chasing the same trends; the 2/20-day crossover paid in the 1980s but no longer.

steps.to: Winton lowers its forecast for trend following year by year and diversifies into equity and other strategies without abandoning it
steps.why: Innovation or decay; but trend following is still expected to make money.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Own 30-year record, the 1980s crossover anecdote, and client communication; no quantified decay estimate is given.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated for decay; he says trend following can still work, it just cannot be relied on.

steps.to: Risk of an overnight systemic move
steps.why: Fat tails; LTCM and 2008 show crowded positions unwinding together.

steps.to: Winton cuts leverage (about 2x gross in long/short portfolios versus ~10x rumoured at others)
steps.why: No responsible professional wants to be implicated in a systemic crisis; more so with unsophisticated clients.

steps.from: Lower leverage and near-zero cash rates
steps.to: Lower headline returns that look similar to the past once adjusted
steps.why: Double the leverage and add 6% cash and the record resembles the past.

mechanism_chains.evidence: LTCM and 2008 episodes; arithmetic of adjusting for leverage and cash.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why trend following is not a crash hedge

steps.from: Trend systems are long equity indices after rallies
steps.to: A sudden fall hits CTAs long
steps.why: Signals follow past trends; in Feb 2018 managed futures were long after three months of highs.

steps.to: Trend following gains and can act as a hedge
steps.why: Trends establish themselves before the bulk of the loss.

steps.from: Volatility spikes after calm (2007, 2016 vol derivatives, 2018)
steps.to: Returns hurt and no way to solve for it
steps.why: Stock markets go up and down a lot; short-lived shocks cannot be anticipated.

mechanism_chains.fails_when: A 1987 or Feb 2018 style fast crash; 'one swallow does not make a summer'.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why government macro data are a poor systematic input

steps.from: Statistics are revised often and over long periods
steps.to: The meaning of historical series changes and real-time prints differ from final data
steps.why: US 2009 double dip erased nine years later; two Japanese growth estimates, 0.4 vs 2.5.

steps.to: Long-term tests of fundamental data (e.g. PMI) produce nothing provable after years of work
steps.why: Too little data; sunk cost should not force a result.

steps.to: Global macro that relies on government data is hard to systematise
steps.why: Estimates differ and cannot be trusted.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Two years and several million pounds spent on a PMI study that was inconclusive.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated; he does not rule out signals in other data (e.g. weather in ag futures).

mechanism_chains.topic: Moving into global equities (and other markets) via compute and data

steps.to: Much larger portfolios (7,000 stocks, up from 1,000-1,500) and high-frequency data used to measure correlation changes and new factors
steps.why: Rent huge computation for short experiments instead of owning machines.

steps.to: A third to a half of weight in equity strategies (event, organizational metrics, customised technical)
steps.why: Equity-specific strategies are needed; momentum know-how transfers partly.

steps.from: Capacity limits in markets like agricultural futures
steps.to: Only very long-term strategies there; research on weather and 1,200-year grain series is exploratory
steps.why: Large capital cannot trade in and out without moving the market.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Own operations; no performance data given for the equity book.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated; interviewer raises doubts that a trend firm can carry across to equities.

decision_process.practice: Futures trend following kept but de-emphasised; equity strategies are event strategies, organizational/governance metric strategies, and technical strategies customised to the 7,000-stock universe.
decision_process.why: Edge in simple futures trend decayed; futures rules do not carry over to equities.

decision_process.practice: Global portfolio of about 7,000 stocks (from 1,000-1,500 five years earlier), plus futures including a long-horizon agricultural futures project.
decision_process.why: Cloud computing makes bigger universes tractable; ag futures offer a niche if long-term strategies fit within capacity.

decision_process.practice: Hire and train many scientists, build huge databases, run patient cumulative research shared internally but not published; use short-term high-frequency data for monitoring correlations and new factors though trading is long term.
decision_process.why: Edge comes from cumulative science (the Renaissance analogy); no IP protection so secrecy.

decision_process.practice: Stop a research project when evidence cannot be established; do not let sunk cost force a result (the PMI study cost about two years and several million pounds).
decision_process.why: Avoid forcing signals from unproven data.

decision_process.practice: Set portfolio volatility with a single leverage 'volume knob' (10, 20 or 30 vol) as a commercial decision independent of strategy.
decision_process.why: Volatility target is a client/commercial choice, not a property of the signal.

decision_process.practice: Conservative leverage: about 2x gross in long/short portfolios, far below the ~10x rumoured at competitors, and more so for less sophisticated clients.
decision_process.why: Crowding plus fat tails creates catastrophe risk.

decision_process.practice: Diversify away from sole reliance on trend following into other statistical strategies, knowing none can be timed; judge over years, not months.
decision_process.why: All such strategies are unpredictable but have objective grounds for long-term profit; diversification helps.

decision_process.practice: Fully systematic book: researchers write and run the programs, separate teams handle 24-hour execution, and humans intervene only to correct program errors; named humans remain responsible.
decision_process.why: Responsibility must stay with people, not 'the computer'.

decision_process.practice: Match liquidity terms to assets: fund redemption terms moved to monthly notice and annual performance-fee crystallisation as small-company equity holdings grew; fees cut to 0.9% and 16%.
decision_process.why: Returns did not justify fees; liquidity should match the assets.

decision_process.practice: Spin off data cleaning as Hivemind and rent cloud compute for large one-off experiments.
decision_process.why: Clean data are the unglamorous prerequisite of research; renting 50,000 computers for a minute avoids owning machines.

decision_process.practice: Stay exclusively focused on managing client money (no proprietary book), presented as an alignment advantage for institutions, and aspire to be seen alongside the large US systematic quant firms.
decision_process.why: Institutions value alignment; doubts exist whether a firm from a trend-following tradition can carry across into equities.

speakers.evidence_style: Long track record and personal history (nearly 40 years, a Sharpe near 1 for 30 years), historical episodes (LTCM, 2008, 1987, Feb 2018), data-revision anecdotes, and analogies (jungle vs atoms, science as cumulative research, Renaissance). He cites few quantitative tests, and says his PMI study was inconclusive rather than negative.

current_views.view: Trend following in futures has become crowded and should be expected to earn less; Winton lowers its forecast but still expects it to make money, and diversifies rather than abandoning it.
current_views.reasoning: Too much money and competition; the strategy is seen as accessible beta.

current_views.view: Systematic quant has a bigger future in 20 years because markets will not become efficient, and the word 'quant' will eventually be dropped as all investing uses computers.
current_views.reasoning: Inefficiencies persist; competition is fierce but not monopolistic.

current_views.view: Managed futures trend following is not a dependable hedge against equity crashes.
current_views.reasoning: Long positions after rallies (Feb 2018); 1987-style fall would not be hedged.

current_views.view: Market volatility is not structurally rising; the idea that it is comes from using nominal point charts rather than percent charts.
current_views.reasoning: 1933-34 percent volatility was the highest ever.

current_views.view: Hedge fund industry returns have been sustained by the equity bull market's spillover, and returns are thin; many discretionary managers without real edge face a bad future.
current_views.reasoning: Biggest bull market in history in dollar terms to last year; more data and performance evaluation; automation of simple discretionary rules.

current_views.view: Government macro data are not trustworthy enough for systematic global macro.
AI is mostly hype for now; discoveries will come but their significance cannot be ordered.
current_views.reasoning: Deep learning progress is narrow; discoveries are science, not on demand.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: He says trend following has decayed and is crowded, yet still expects it to make money and says the new strategies have 'the same properties'; no quantified decay or expected Sharpe is given for either.
No evidence is offered that the new equity strategies outperform; he says the shift has not yet been shown to deliver better returns and that nobody should judge a month or year.

He argues the Sharpe-near-1 claim and then that trend following has nothing to do with intelligence (a simple algorithm made ~15% for 20 years); the 15% figure is unqualified and may be gross of the fees and leverage effects he mentions.
Tension: he says volatility spikes (2016, 2018) hurt returns and cannot be solved for, but also that the volume knob makes volatility a commercial choice independent of strategy.
Claim that percent volatility peaked in 1933-34 is recalled from memory and not sourced in the interview.
Reasoning that crowding is the driver of lower returns competes with his own adjustment argument (cash rates and leverage); both are offered without separating the effects.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Harding names no short-horizon predictive indicator. The inputs he treats as leading future returns are: how crowded a strategy is (money in it, whether it is viewed as beta), interest rate level (cash component of returns), leverage and fat-tail risk from crowding, and whether time series are clean enough to prove an effect (government data often are not). Horizons are years to decades; he stresses that no month or year judges a manager.
reader_inferences: (reader) Harding's crowding thesis predicts that returns of an openly published, easily replicated rule (simple trend) trend toward cash-like or beta-like outcomes over time, which is testable by rolling Sharpe of managed-futures indices against assets under management.

(reader) His claim that trend following is not a crash hedge implies it should be treated as a convex-in-slow-trends, not in fast-gap, instrument; the testable form is conditional returns on speed of equity drawdowns.
(reader) The case for equity event and organizational-metric strategies versus futures trend is a diversification and capacity argument, not backed by reported returns in this interview.
(reader) His distrust of revised macro data matches the point-in-time / first-release data problem in macro research.
